hero.identity: I’m Théo Phan, a computer science student at INSA Rennes. I like building apps and learning how they behave outside a demo.
hero.headline: I build things that need to work.
hero.portraitAlt: Théo Phan smiling and holding a phone

status.headline: I like figuring out why something fails, then trying to make it work.

principles.title: Start with the parts
principles.text: Sometimes I rebuild what a library could do, once, so I understand what is happening underneath.

principles.title: Test on the mess
principles.text: Real phones, imperfect photos, and bad networks are where the useful problems begin.

principles.title: Keep the evidence
principles.text: A working demo is a start. I want to know what changed and whether the fix holds.

experience.headline: A path, not a checklist.
experience.intro: Each step made the next question a little more ambitious, and a little closer to the physical world.

projects.heading: Selected work
projects.intro: A few things I have made and learned from.
projects.outro: There are more experiments, useful tools, and ideas that got slightly out of hand.

01.question: What if self-control had a physical shape?
01.note: I led three students from a stubborn idea to a product people now carry in their pockets.
01.result: Live on iOS + Android · 1,425+ units sold

09.question: Could a document quietly hijack an AI?
09.note: Reading about prompt injection felt too comfortable, so I built a vulnerable assistant and attacked it myself.

10.question: What is a neural network hiding from me?
10.note: I built the DQN training loop in Rust and watched the agent slowly teach itself to survive.

03.question: Can a model cope with the mess outside a lab?
03.note: I compared vision models on imperfect plant photos to find the point where a benchmark becomes genuinely useful.

hobbies.heading: Photography
hobbies.body: Photography makes me slow down and notice geometry, light, and the one detail that changes the frame. It is the opposite of debugging, and somehow the same skill.

01.intro: Hübner drew a specimen, named it, and placed it in a taxonomy. Two hundred years later, the same problem answered by a model on photographs taken in a field.
01.historicalAlt: An 1806 engraving of a moth with its wings spread, printed as a halftone plate
01.historicalCaption: Plate I. Jacob Hübner, Sammlung exotischer Schmetterlinge, Augsburg, 1806.
01.historicalNote: Drawn from the specimen, named, and placed in a taxonomy by eye.
01.evidenceAlt: Apple leaves under detection boxes labelled Apple Scab Leaf, with confidence scores up to 0.94
01.evidenceCaption: Plate II. Plant Detection, YOLOv8, 2025. mAP@50 0.90, recall 85.8%.
01.evidenceNote: Found, boxed and scored at 0.94 confidence on photographs taken in the field.
